satire

SAT-eye-ur — satire pokes fun until the target's pride goes flat. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Satire is a work that uses mockery or exaggeration to expose foolishness.

The magazine's satire of celebrity culture exaggerated every red-carpet cliché until it became absurd.

Example

A comedy sketch shows a fictional politician promising to fix every problem in the world by tomorrow, then getting distracted by a free sandwich. Audiences laugh because it exaggerates a real habit they recognize in real politicians.

Using exaggeration and mockery to point out a real, ridiculous flaw is exactly what satire does. Unlike 'insult,' which is direct and personal, satire uses humor and exaggeration to make its point.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

parody: A parody is a comically exaggerated imitation of a specific work or style, made for the fun of the imitation itself. Satire borrows the same tools — exaggeration, mockery — but aims them at a real flaw in politics or society, exposing foolishness rather than just getting laughs.

mockery: Mockery is ridicule or scornful imitation of any kind, and it needs no craft — a sneer can be mockery. Satire is a made thing: a sketch, cartoon, or piece of writing that shapes its mockery into a work designed to expose real foolishness.

lampoon: A lampoon is a piece of writing that harshly mocks a particular person or institution — the attack is pointed and blunt. Satire can be gentler and wider: it exaggerates a general flaw in society or politics, and its laughter aims at the folly more than at one individual.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

tribute: an act showing respect or admiration

praise: an expression of approval or admiration

Where it sits · how harshly the flaw is attacked — irony → satire → ridicule

irony vs. satire: Irony is milder than satire — irony simply points out a contradiction, while satire goes further, actively mocking and exaggerating a flaw to expose it.

ridicule vs. satire: Ridicule can be stronger than satire: satire often uses humor and cleverness to make its point, but ridicule can be blunt, harsh mockery with no cleverness at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — satur-

root — satur-: full, mixed (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Satire traces back to Latin satira or satura, originally meaning a 'medley' or 'mixture' of verse forms; the exact path to today's meaning of mocking exaggeration is debated by etymologists.

Use the root in a new word: saturate

Use the root in a new word: saturate: The heavy rain began to saturate the soil until it could not absorb any more water.
